items.question: A blue triangle has a dotted line down its middle. If you fold the triangle along the dotted line, does one half cover the other half completely? Now look at four puzzle pieces joined together with a dotted line through the middle. Are the two sides mirror halves?
steps: Fold the triangle along the dotted line: the halves match exactly.
Fold the puzzle pieces along their dotted line: the bumps and holes on the two sides do not match.
Only an exact match gives mirror halves.
items.answer: For the triangle: yes, one half covers the other exactly, so they are mirror halves. For the puzzle pieces: no, when folded along the line the left half does not exactly fit over the right half.

videos.answer: For the triangle: yes, one half covers the other exactly, so they are mirror halves. For the puzzle pieces: no, when folded along the line the left half does not exactly fit over the right half.

items.question: Look at the pictures of the Taj Mahal and the Gopuram (a temple tower). What are the symmetries that you see in these beautiful structures? Why is the picture of the clouds not symmetrical?
steps: Imagine a vertical line down the middle of each building.
Check that the left side matches the right side.
Clouds have no repeating pattern, so no symmetry.
items.answer: Each of the Taj Mahal and the Gopuram has a vertical line down the middle with the left half matching the right half, and many parts repeat in a pattern (towers, windows, tiers). The clouds have no repeating pattern, so they are not symmetrical.

videos.answer: Each of the Taj Mahal and the Gopuram has a vertical line down the middle with the left half matching the right half, and many parts repeat in a pattern (towers, windows, tiers). The clouds have no repeating pattern, so they are not symmetrical.

items.question: Do you see any line of symmetry in the pictures at the start of the chapter (flower, butterfly, rangoli, pinwheel)? What about the picture of the cloud?
steps: Try folding each picture along different lines.
Count the lines where the two halves match exactly: flower 6, rangoli 4, butterfly 1.
The pinwheel looks symmetric but its halves do not match when folded, and the cloud has no pattern.
items.answer: Yes: the flower has 6 lines of symmetry, the rangoli has 4, and the butterfly has 1. The pinwheel and the cloud have no line of symmetry.

videos.answer: Yes: the flower has 6 lines of symmetry, the rangoli has 4, and the butterfly has 1. The pinwheel and the cloud have no line of symmetry.

items.question: For each of the following figures, identify the line(s) of symmetry if it exists. The five figures, in order, are: (1) an irregular pentagon-like shape with a notch (arrow-head like), (2) a kite, (3) a quadrilateral with two right angles and a slanted top, (4) an L-shape, (5) a scalene triangle. 1) Arrow-head like pentagon with a notch 2) Kite 3) Quadrilateral with slanted top and two right angles 4) L-shape 5) Scalene triangle
steps: Fold each shape in your mind and look for a line that makes both halves match.
The kite folds along its vertical diagonal; the L-shape folds along the diagonal through its corner.
The slanted quadrilateral and the scalene triangle have no matching fold.
items.answer: Shape 1 has one line of symmetry (a slanted line through its tip). Shape 2 (kite) has one vertical line of symmetry. Shape 3 has none. Shape 4 (L-shape) has one diagonal line of symmetry through its corner. Shape 5 (scalene triangle) has none.

videos.answer: Shape 1 has one line of symmetry (a slanted line through its tip). Shape 2 (kite) has one vertical line of symmetry. Shape 3 has none. Shape 4 (L-shape) has one diagonal line of symmetry through its corner. Shape 5 (scalene triangle) has none.

source: Does a square have only one line of symmetry? Take a square

items.question: Does a square have only one line of symmetry? Take a square piece of paper and, by folding, find all its lines of symmetry.
steps: Fold the square in half vertically, then horizontally.
Fold it along one diagonal, then along the other diagonal.
Each fold makes the two halves overlap exactly, so there are 4 lines.
items.answer: No. A square has 4 lines of symmetry: a vertical fold, a horizontal fold, and the two diagonals.

videos.answer: No. A square has 4 lines of symmetry: a vertical fold, a horizontal fold, and the two diagonals.

source: Is there any other way to fold the square so that the two ha

items.question: Is there any other way to fold the square so that the two halves overlap? How many lines of symmetry does the square shape have?
steps: The four folds are the vertical, horizontal and the two diagonals.
No other fold line makes the halves overlap.
So the count is 4.
items.answer: No, there is no other way to fold the square. A square has 4 lines of symmetry.

videos.answer: No, there is no other way to fold the square. A square has 4 lines of symmetry.

source: Find all the lines of symmetry of each of three figures: (1)

items.question: Find all the lines of symmetry of each of three figures: (1) a red outline ring with spiky triangular points around it (like a Koch snowflake), (2) a yellow flower of six curved petals meeting at a red-marked centre, (3) a green looped design with four round loops at the corners and a small square in the centre.
steps: Fold each figure in your mind along vertical, horizontal and slanted lines.
Count the lines where both halves match.
The twisted petal flower never matches its mirror image, so no line.
items.answer: Figure 1: 6 lines. Figure 2: no line of symmetry (it only has rotational symmetry). Figure 3: 4 lines (vertical, horizontal and the two diagonals).

videos.answer: Figure 1: 6 lines. Figure 2: no line of symmetry (it only has rotational symmetry). Figure 3: 4 lines (vertical, horizontal and the two diagonals).

source: We saw that the diagonal of a square is also a line of symme

items.question: We saw that the diagonal of a square is also a line of symmetry. Take a rectangle that is not a square. Is its diagonal a line of symmetry? First see the rectangle and answer, then take a rectangular piece of paper and check by folding along its diagonal whether the two parts overlap.
steps: Cut a rectangle that is longer than it is wide.
Fold along a diagonal.
The corners and sides do not meet, so the halves do not overlap.
items.answer: No. The diagonal of a rectangle that is not a square is not a line of symmetry: when folded along the diagonal the two parts do not overlap.

videos.answer: No. The diagonal of a rectangle that is not a square is not a line of symmetry: when folded along the diagonal the two parts do not overlap.

items.question: How many lines of symmetry do these shapes have? (a) a square drawn tilted like a diamond, and an eight-pointed star shape; (b) a triangle with equal sides and equal angles; (c) a hexagon with equal sides and equal angles. a) square drawn like a diamond; eight-pointed star b) triangle with equal sides and equal angles c) hexagon with equal sides and equal angles
steps: For a regular shape, the number of lines equals the number of sides.
A square has 4, an equilateral triangle 3 and a regular hexagon 6.
The eight-pointed star has 8 lines through its points and notches.
items.answer: (a) tilted square: 4; eight-pointed star: 8. (b) equilateral triangle: 3. (c) regular hexagon: 6.

videos.answer: (a) tilted square: 4; eight-pointed star: 8. (b) equilateral triangle: 3. (c) regular hexagon: 6.

items.question: Trace each figure and draw the lines of symmetry, if any. There are eight figures: four rhombus-pattern figures (1: one rhombus sitting on top of two rhombi that touch each other; 2: three rhombi in a row joined at their left-right corners; 3: a large diamond made of four small rhombi; 4: four rhombi in two columns of two, overlapping, standing in an X-like arrangement) and four figures on squared grids (5: a square inside a bigger square with the inner square divided into four; 6: an octagon-like shape with long vertical sides; 7: a five-sided shape like a kite with a flat right side; 8: a four-pointed star). 1) rhombus pattern 1 (one rhombus above two) 2) three rhombi in a row 3) large diamond of four rhombi 4) four overlapping rhombi, two columns 5) square inside a square on grid 6) octagon-like shape on grid 7) five-sided shape on grid 8) four-pointed star on grid
steps: Trace the figure on paper or imagine folding it.
Try vertical, horizontal and diagonal folds.
Count the folds where the two halves overlap.
items.answer: 1: 1 line (vertical). 2: 2 lines (horizontal and vertical). 3: 2 lines (horizontal and vertical). 4: 2 lines (horizontal and vertical). 5: 4 lines (vertical, horizontal and the two diagonals). 6: 2 lines (vertical and horizontal). 7: 1 line (horizontal). 8: 4 lines (vertical, horizontal and two diagonals).

videos.answer: 1: 1 line (vertical). 2: 2 lines (horizontal and vertical). 3: 2 lines (horizontal and vertical). 4: 2 lines (horizontal and vertical). 5: 4 lines (vertical, horizontal and the two diagonals). 6: 2 lines (vertical and horizontal). 7: 1 line (horizontal). 8: 4 lines (vertical, horizontal and two diagonals).

items.question: Find the lines of symmetry for the kolam below. The kolam is a large six-sided (hexagonal) pattern made of dots and star shapes made of rhombi, with the same design repeating around the centre.
steps: Look for lines through the centre where one side matches the other.
The pattern repeats 6 times around the centre, so there are 6 lines.
items.answer: The kolam has 6 lines of symmetry: one vertical line, one horizontal line and four slanted lines, all through the centre.

videos.answer: The kolam has 6 lines of symmetry: one vertical line, one horizontal line and four slanted lines, all through the centre.

items.question: Draw the following. (a) A triangle with exactly one line of symmetry. (b) A triangle with exactly three lines of symmetry. (c) A triangle with no line of symmetry. Is it possible to draw a triangle with exactly two lines of symmetry? a) triangle with exactly one line of symmetry b) triangle with exactly three lines of symmetry c) triangle with no line of symmetry d) Is it possible to draw a triangle with exactly two lines of symmetry?
steps: Two equal sides give one line: the line from the apex to the middle of the base.
All three sides equal give three lines.
If a triangle has two lines of symmetry it is forced to have all three, so exactly two cannot happen.
items.answer: (a) An isosceles triangle (two equal sides, third side different). (b) An equilateral triangle. (c) A scalene triangle (all sides different). No, it is not possible to draw a triangle with exactly two lines of symmetry.

videos.answer: (a) An isosceles triangle (two equal sides, third side different). (b) An equilateral triangle. (c) A scalene triangle (all sides different). No, it is not possible to draw a triangle with exactly two lines of symmetry.

items.question: Draw the following. In each case, the figure should contain at least one curved boundary. (a) A figure with exactly one line of symmetry. (b) A figure with exactly two lines of symmetry. (c) A figure with exactly four lines of symmetry. a) exactly one line of symmetry, with a curved boundary b) exactly two lines of symmetry, with a curved boundary c) exactly four lines of symmetry, with a curved boundary
steps: Start with a symmetric shape such as a square or an arrow shape.
Replace some edges by curves, placing the same curve on each matching side.
Count the lines to check.
items.answer: Any correct drawing works. Example: (a) a semicircle (one line, perpendicular to the straight edge) or a shape with a round top and a symmetrical body; (b) an ellipse or a rectangle with rounded bumps at the top and bottom (vertical and horizontal lines); (c) a circle-bump flower of four equal round loops around a square (4 lines).

videos.answer: Any correct drawing works. Example: (a) a semicircle (one line, perpendicular to the straight edge) or a shape with a round top and a symmetrical body; (b) an ellipse or a rectangle with rounded bumps at the top and bottom (vertical and horizontal lines); (c) a circle-bump flower of four equal round loops around a square (4 lines).

source: A square has corners labelled A (top left), B (top right), C

items.question: A square has corners labelled A (top left), B (top right), C (bottom right), D (bottom left). When the square is reflected along the vertical line of symmetry, where do A, B, C and D go?
steps: Draw the vertical line through the middle.
Each corner moves to the matching corner on the other side of the line, at the same height.
items.answer: B and C go to the positions earlier held by A and D, and A and D go to the positions earlier held by B and C: A takes the place of B, B the place of A, D the place of C and C the place of D.

videos.answer: B and C go to the positions earlier held by A and D, and A and D go to the positions earlier held by B and C: A takes the place of B, B the place of A, D the place of C and C the place of D.

source: For the same square ABCD (A top left, B top right, C bottom

items.question: For the same square ABCD (A top left, B top right, C bottom right, D bottom left): what if we reflect along the diagonal from A to C? Where do points A, B, C and D go? What if we reflect along the horizontal line of symmetry?
steps: Points on the line of symmetry stay where they are.
A point off the line goes to the matching point on the other side, at the same distance from the line.
For the diagonal AC, B and D are on opposite sides, so they swap.
For the horizontal line, the top corners swap with the bottom corners.
items.answer: Along diagonal AC: A and C stay where they are, and B and D swap places (D takes B's earlier position and B takes D's). Along the horizontal line: A and D swap places, and B and C swap places (D and C take the places of A and B, and A and B take the places of D and C).

videos.answer: Along diagonal AC: A and C stay where they are, and B and D swap places (D takes B's earlier position and B takes D's). Along the horizontal line: A and D swap places, and B and C swap places (D and C take the places of A and B, and A and B take the places of D and C).

items.question: Copy the following on squared paper. Complete them so that the blue line is a line of symmetry. Problem (a) has been done for you. (b) A stepped red shape above a horizontal blue line, with a slanted edge ending at the right end of the line. (c) A staircase-shaped red outline next to a slanted (diagonal) blue line. (d) A small red shape touching a vertical blue line on a narrow grid. (e) A red five-sided outline hanging below a horizontal blue line. (f) A red outline with corner cuts next to a diagonal blue line. Hint: for (c) and (f), see if rotating the book helps! b) red stepped shape above a horizontal blue line c) staircase outline beside a diagonal blue line d) small shape on a vertical line e) five-sided red outline hanging below a horizontal line f) red outline with corner cuts beside a diagonal line
steps: Pick a corner of the red outline and count its distance from the blue line.
Go the same distance on the other side and mark the mirror corner.
Join the mirror corners in the same order.
For a diagonal line, turn the page so that the line is vertical or horizontal.
items.answer: In each case, reflect every point of the red outline in the blue line: draw each mirror point at the same distance on the other side, then join the mirror points. The finished shape is symmetric about the blue line. (b) the shape is mirrored below the horizontal line; (c) mirrored across the diagonal; (d) the left red part is mirrored to the right of the vertical line; (e) mirrored above the horizontal line; (f) mirrored across the diagonal.

The finished shape is symmetric about the blue line. items.question: Copy the following drawing on squared paper. Complete each one of them so that the resulting figure has the two blue lines as lines of symmetry. (a) two diagonal blue lines crossing, with a red horizontal segment near the bottom; (b) two diagonal blue lines crossing, with a red broken vertical segment with a point on the left; (c) a vertical and a horizontal blue line, with a stepped red outline in the upper left; (d) a vertical and a horizontal blue line, with a red corner outline in the lower left; (e) a vertical and a horizontal blue line, with a red zigzag in the upper right; (f) a vertical and a horizontal blue line, with a red outline in the lower left. a) diagonals, red bottom segment b) diagonals, red left zigzag c) vertical and horizontal, stepped upper-left outline d) vertical and horizontal, lower-left corner outline e) vertical and horizontal, upper-right zigzag f) vertical and horizontal, lower-left outline
steps: Reflect the given red part in one blue line.
Reflect the new figure (old plus new) in the other blue line.
Check that both blue lines now act as folds.
items.answer: Reflect the red part in the first blue line, then reflect the whole result in the second blue line. Then the figure is symmetric about both. (a) completes to a square; (b) completes to a four-sided figure with an arrow-head point on each side; (c) a symmetric cross-like stepped shape; (d) a symmetric octagon-like shape; (e) a symmetric stepped cross shape with a notched top and bottom; (f) a symmetric butterfly-like shape.

videos.answer: Reflect the red part in the first blue line, then reflect the whole result in the second blue line. Then the figure is symmetric about both. (a) completes to a square; (b) completes to a four-sided figure with an arrow-head point on each side; (c) a symmetric cross-like stepped shape; (d) a symmetric octagon-like shape; (e) a symmetric stepped cross shape with a notched top and bottom; (f) a symmetric butterfly-like shape.

The solutions show closed shapes (four-sided or five-sided) each with one drawn line of symmetry.

source: Take a piece of paper and fold it in half. Open it and spill

items.question: Take a piece of paper and fold it in half. Open it and spill a few drops of ink (or paint) on one half. Press the halves together and open the paper again. What do you see? Is the resulting figure symmetric? If yes, where is the line of symmetry? Is there any other line along which it can be folded to produce two identical parts? Try making more such patterns.
steps: Fold the paper in half and put ink on one half.
Press the halves together and open: the ink prints a mirror image on the other half.
The crease is the line of symmetry.
items.answer: You see a blot pattern with the same shape on both sides of the crease. Yes, it is symmetric and the fold (crease) is the line of symmetry. Usually no other line works, since the shape is random, so there is just one line of symmetry.

videos.answer: You see a blot pattern with the same shape on both sides of the crease. Yes, it is symmetric and the fold (crease) is the line of symmetry. Usually no other line works, since the shape is random, so there is just one line of symmetry.

source: In two pictures, a sheet of paper is folded and a cut is mad

items.question: In two pictures, a sheet of paper is folded and a cut is made along the dotted line shown (the dotted line forms a notch shape starting at the fold). Draw a sketch of how the paper will look when unfolded. Do you see a line of symmetry in this figure? What is it?
steps: Imagine opening the folded sheet.
The cut shape appears on both sides of the crease, as mirror images.
The crease is the line of symmetry.
items.answer: The unfolded paper has a hole (or cut-out) whose shape is the cut shape and its mirror image joined together along the fold. Yes, the fold line is the line of symmetry.

videos.answer: The unfolded paper has a hole (or cut-out) whose shape is the cut shape and its mirror image joined together along the fold. Yes, the fold line is the line of symmetry.

items.question: Make different symmetric shapes by folding and cutting. Use thin rectangular coloured paper, fold it several times and cut out intricate patterns, like the blue star-shaped cut-outs shown. Identify the lines of symmetry in the repeating design.
steps: Fold the paper several times.
Cut some shapes along the edges and corners.
Open it: every crease is a line of symmetry of the repeating design.
items.answer: Any such cut-out is symmetric about each of its fold lines. For example, the eight-pointed star shown has 8 lines of symmetry.

items.question: In each of the following figures, a hole was punched in a folded square sheet of paper and then the paper was unfolded. Identify the line along which the paper was folded. The four unfolded sheets show: (a) two holes in the left and right sides at the same height; (b) two holes close together near the top right corner; (c) two holes on the right edge, one above the other; (d) four holes, one near each corner. Figure (d) was created by punching a single hole. How was the paper folded? a) two holes, one on the left and one on the right at the same height b) two holes close together near the top right corner c) two holes on the right edge, one above the other d) four holes near the four corners (made with a single hole)
steps: The fold line is the line of symmetry, halfway between each pair of matching holes and at right angles to the line joining them.
For (d), four holes means two lines of symmetry: fold in half, then in half again.
items.answer: (a) a vertical fold through the middle; (b) a diagonal fold (from bottom left to top right) between the two holes; (c) a horizontal fold through the middle between the two holes; (d) the paper was folded vertically and then horizontally (or the other way round), and one hole was punched through all four layers.

videos.answer: (a) a vertical fold through the middle; (b) a diagonal fold (from bottom left to top right) between the two holes; (c) a horizontal fold through the middle between the two holes; (d) the paper was folded vertically and then horizontally (or the other way round), and one hole was punched through all four layers.

items.question: Given the line(s) of symmetry, find the other hole(s). Five shapes each show one hole and a dashed line of symmetry: (a) a square with a diagonal from top left to bottom right and a hole near the top left; (b) a square with a horizontal middle line and a hole in the lower right; (c) an equilateral triangle with a vertical line through the apex and a hole just left of the line near the middle; (d) a circle with a slanted diameter and a hole above the line near the right; (e) a circle with a diagonal line from top left to bottom right and a hole near the top left, close to the line. a) square, diagonal line, hole near top left b) square, horizontal middle line, hole lower right c) triangle, vertical line, hole left of the line d) circle, slanted diameter, hole above the line e) circle, diagonal line, hole near top left
steps: Draw a line from the given hole that meets the dashed line at a right angle.
Go the same distance past the dashed line.
Mark the new hole there.
items.answer: In every shape the other hole is the mirror image of the given hole in the dashed line: same distance from the line, on the opposite side. (a) the other hole is across the diagonal, near the top edge; (b) in the upper right, directly above the given hole; (c) to the right of the vertical line at the same height; (d) below the slanted line, mirrored; (e) on the other side of the diagonal, mirrored.

videos.answer: In every shape the other hole is the mirror image of the given hole in the dashed line: same distance from the line, on the opposite side. (a) the other hole is across the diagonal, near the top edge; (b) in the upper right, directly above the given hole; (c) to the right of the vertical line at the same height; (d) below the slanted line, mirrored; (e) on the other side of the diagonal, mirrored.

items.question: Suppose you have to get each of these shapes with some folds and a single straight cut. How will you do it? (a) The hole in the centre is a square (sides parallel to the sides of the sheet). (b) The hole in the centre is a square (tilted so that its corners point up, down, left and right). Note: for the above two questions, check if the 4-sided figures in the centre satisfy both the properties of a square. a) square hole in the centre with sides parallel to the paper b) tilted square hole in the centre
steps: Fold twice so that the centre of the sheet is at one corner of the small folded square.
For (a) cut off a small square at that corner.
For (b) cut a slanting line across that corner, removing a triangle.
Open the sheet: the four mirror copies join to make the hole.
items.answer: (a) Fold the paper horizontally and then vertically. At the closed corner (the corner that is the centre of the sheet) cut a small square with all sides closed, using straight cuts parallel to the folds. (b) Fold the paper horizontally and then vertically. At the closed corner cut along one slanting (diagonal) line so that a small triangle is removed; opening gives a tilted square.

videos.answer: (a) Fold the paper horizontally and then vertically. At the closed corner (the corner that is the centre of the sheet) cut a small square with all sides closed, using straight cuts parallel to the folds. (b) Fold the paper horizontally and then vertically. At the closed corner cut along one slanting (diagonal) line so that a small triangle is removed; opening gives a tilted square.

items.question: Look at the rangoli picture (a round flower-like design with a ring in the centre and four red petals around it). Can you see what repeats in it? What happens to the red petals when the rangoli is rotated by 90° around the centre?
steps: Look at the red petals around the centre.
Turn the picture by 90° (a quarter turn) about the centre.
Each petal lands exactly on the next petal, so the pattern repeats.
items.answer: The same petal shape repeats around the centre. When the rangoli is turned by 90° about its centre, the red petals come back exactly onto themselves, and so do the other parts.

steps: A shape with 4 angles of symmetry matches itself after each quarter turn.
A square does this: 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°.
A plus sign with 4 equal arms does the same.
items.answer: Yes, a square (also a plus sign made of 4 equal arms, or a pinwheel with 4 equal blades).

source: How many angles of symmetry does a square have? How much rot

items.question: How many angles of symmetry does a square have? How much rotation does it require to get the initial square?
steps: Rotate the square about its centre by a quarter turn: it overlaps itself.
Each further quarter turn does the same: 90°, 180°, 270°.
A full turn of 360° brings every corner back to its own place.
items.answer: 4 angles of symmetry: 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°. The square overlaps itself after a 90° rotation (A goes to B, B to C, C to D, D to A); it is back in its starting position after 360°.

items.question: A square gets back onto itself after a 90° rotation. Do you know where to mark the centre of rotation?
steps: The centre of rotation is the fixed point that does not move.
In a square this is the middle point.
It is where the diagonals meet.
items.answer: At the centre of the square, the point where its two diagonals cross.

videos.answer: At the centre of the square, the point where its two diagonals cross.

items.question: What are the other angles of symmetry of a square (besides 90°)?
steps: Rotate the square by 180° (half turn): it overlaps itself.
Rotate by 270° (three-quarter turn): it overlaps itself.
Rotate by 360° (full turn): it is back where it started.

source: Find the angles of symmetry of the following strip. The stri

items.question: Find the angles of symmetry of the following strip. The strip is a trapezium shape (the top side is shorter than the bottom side, the two slanting sides are equal) with a dot marking its centre.
steps: Rotate the strip by 180° about its centre: the longer side is now on top.
This does not overlap the original, because the top and bottom sides are different.
Another 180° gives the original, so only the full turn 360° works.
items.answer: Only 360°. The strip does not have rotational symmetry.

videos.answer: Only 360°. The strip does not have rotational symmetry.

source: After the strip is rotated by 180° about its centre, does it

items.question: After the strip is rotated by 180° about its centre, does it overlap with the original strip? Why?
steps: Look at the top and bottom sides of the strip.
They are different in length.
A half turn swaps them, so the picture changes.
items.answer: No. After 180° the shorter side is at the bottom and the longer side at the top, so it does not fit the original.

source: A picture has 4 radial arms (a plus-shaped figure with 4 equ

items.question: A picture has 4 radial arms (a plus-shaped figure with 4 equal arms), and the angle between adjacent central dotted lines is 90°. How many angles of symmetry does it have? What are they?
steps: The arms are equal and 90° apart.
Each quarter turn moves an arm onto the next arm.
So the turns 90°, 180°, 270° and 360° all work.
items.answer: 4 angles of symmetry: 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°.

videos.answer: 4 angles of symmetry: 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°.

source: Can you change the angles between the radial arms so that th

items.question: Can you change the angles between the radial arms so that the figure still has 4 angles of symmetry? Try drawing it.
steps: For 4 angles of symmetry, a quarter turn must put each arm on the next arm.
So all four angles between neighbouring arms must be equal.
They must add to 360°, so each is 90°.
items.answer: Not if the arms are identical and only the angles are changed: the 4 arms must stay equally spaced, with 90° between neighbours. Changing the angles gives fewer angles of symmetry.

videos.answer: Not if the arms are identical and only the angles are changed: the 4 arms must stay equally spaced, with 90° between neighbours. Changing the angles gives fewer angles of symmetry.

items.question: To check if a figure with radial arms has 4 angles of symmetry, draw it on two pieces of paper. Cut out the radial arms from one paper, keep the figure on the other paper fixed, and rotate the cutout to check for rotational symmetry.
steps: Draw the figure twice and cut out one copy.
Pin the cutout at the centre and turn it over the other copy.
Count the turns after which it fits exactly.
items.answer: A correct check shows the cutout fits exactly onto the fixed figure at 90°, 180°, 270° and 360° only.

videos.answer: A correct check shows the cutout fits exactly onto the fixed figure at 90°, 180°, 270° and 360° only.

items.question: How will you modify the plus-shaped figure with 4 radial arms so that it has only two angles of symmetry?
steps: Change the figure so a quarter turn no longer fits.
Keep it the same after a half turn (180°).
Then the angles of symmetry are only 180° and 360°.
items.answer: Make opposite arms alike but the two pairs different, for example the book's figure where the top arm bends to the right at its end and the bottom arm bends to the left (a half turn copy), with the left and right arms straight. Then only 180° and 360° work.

videos.answer: Make opposite arms alike but the two pairs different, for example the book's figure where the top arm bends to the right at its end and the bottom arm bends to the left (a half turn copy), with the left and right arms straight. Then only 180° and 360° work.

items.question: Can we get a figure having exactly 3 angles of symmetry? Can you use radial arms for this?
steps: 3 angles of symmetry means 3 turns that fit, including 360°.
3 equal arms at equal gaps share the full turn equally.
Each gap is 360 ÷ 3 = 120°.
items.answer: Yes: use 3 equal radial arms placed 120° apart.

videos.answer: Yes: use 3 equal radial arms placed 120° apart.

videos.answer: Only 360°, so it has no rotational symmetry.

items.question: Can anything in the three-arm figure be changed to make it have 3 angles of symmetry? Can it be done by changing the angles between the dotted lines?

items.question: If a figure with three radial arms has rotational symmetry, a rotated copy must overlap the original. What can you tell about the angles ∠A, ∠B and ∠C between the arms? What must this angle be?
steps: ∠A must overlap ∠B, ∠B must overlap ∠C and ∠C must overlap ∠A.
So the three angles are equal.
They share 360°, so each is 360 ÷ 3 = 120°.

items.question: A 3-arm figure has 120° between adjacent arms. How many angles of rotation does it have and what are they?
steps: After 120° each arm lands on the next arm.
After 240° (120° + 120°) it fits again.
After 360° (120° + 120° + 120°) it is back to the start.

source: Can you draw a figure with radial arms that has a) exactly 5

items.question: Can you draw a figure with radial arms that has a) exactly 5 angles of symmetry, b) 6 angles of symmetry? Also find the angles of symmetry in each case. Hint: Use 5 radial arms for the first case. What should the angle between two adjacent radial arms be? a) Figure with radial arms having exactly 5 angles of symmetry; list the angles. b) Figure with radial arms having 6 angles of symmetry; list the angles.
steps: For n equal arms the gap between neighbours is 360 ÷ n.
5 arms: 360 ÷ 5 = 72°. Multiples of 72° up to 360°.
6 arms: 360 ÷ 6 = 60°. Multiples of 60° up to 360°.

source: Consider a figure with radial arms having exactly 7 angles o

items.question: Consider a figure with radial arms having exactly 7 angles of symmetry. What will be its smallest angle of symmetry? Is the number of degrees a whole number in this case? If not, express it as a mixed fraction.
steps: 7 equal arms share the full turn of 360°.
360 ÷ 7 gives 51 with remainder 3.
So the smallest angle is 51 3/7°, not a whole number.
items.answer: 360 ÷ 7 is 51 3/7°. It is not a whole number.

videos.answer: 360 ÷ 7 is 51 3/7°. It is not a whole number.

source: Angles of symmetry when there are exactly 2 of them: 180°, 3

items.question: Angles of symmetry when there are exactly 2 of them: 180°, 360°. Exactly 3 of them: 120°, 240°, 360°. Exactly 4 of them: 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°. In each case, the angles are the multiples of the smallest angle. Will this always happen? What do you think?
steps: Turning by the smallest angle twice is the same as turning by twice that angle.
So every angle of symmetry is a multiple of the smallest one.
items.answer: Yes, the angles of symmetry are always multiples of the smallest angle of symmetry.

videos.answer: Yes, the angles of symmetry are always multiples of the smallest angle of symmetry.

source: True or False: (1) Every figure will have 360 degrees as an

items.question: True or False: (1) Every figure will have 360 degrees as an angle of symmetry. (2) If the smallest angle of symmetry of a figure is a natural number in degrees, then it is a factor of 360. 1) Every figure will have 360 degrees as an angle of symmetry. 2) If the smallest angle of symmetry of a figure is a natural number in degrees, then it is a factor of 360.
steps: A full turn of 360° always brings any figure back to itself.
The smallest angle fits a whole number of times in 360°.
So a whole-number smallest angle is a factor of 360.
items.answer: Both are True.

videos.answer: Both are True.

items.question: Colour the sectors of the circle below so that the figure has i) 3 angles of symmetry, ii) 4 angles of symmetry, iii) what are the possible numbers of angles of symmetry you can obtain by colouring the sectors in different ways? The circle is divided into 12 equal sectors. i) 3 angles of symmetry ii) 4 angles of symmetry iii) Possible numbers of angles of symmetry
steps: Each sector is 360 ÷ 12 = 30°.
3 angles of symmetry need a pattern that repeats every 120°, that is every 4 sectors; 4 angles need a pattern repeating every 90°, every 3 sectors.
The pattern can repeat every 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 or 12 sectors, giving 12, 6, 4, 3, 2 or 1 angles of symmetry.
items.answer: i) Colour every 4th sector (3 coloured sectors, 120° apart). ii) Colour every 3rd sector (4 coloured sectors, 90° apart). iii) The number of angles of symmetry can be 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 or 12 (at most 12).

items.question: Can we have a figure with rotational symmetry whose smallest angle of symmetry is: a. 45°? b. 17°? a) Smallest angle of symmetry 45° b) Smallest angle of symmetry 17°
steps: The smallest angle must fit a whole number of times into 360°.
(a) 360 ÷ 45 = 8, so yes: 8 equal arms.
(b) 360 ÷ 17 is not a whole number (17 is not a factor of 360), so no.

items.question: Is there a smallest angle of symmetry for all figures?
steps: A figure like a square has smallest angle 90°.

items.answer: No. Most figures have one, but a circle does not: every angle is an angle of symmetry for a circle.

items.question: Draw, wherever possible, a rough sketch of: a. A triangle with at least two lines of symmetry and at least two angles of symmetry. b. steps: (a) Only an equilateral triangle has 2 or more lines.
(b) An isosceles triangle folds one way only and fits only after 360°.
(c) A slanted parallelogram fits after a half turn but cannot be folded. (d) An isosceles trapezium folds down the middle but a half turn does not fit.

source: Draw a 6 by 6 grid. Two players take turns covering two adja

items.question: Draw a 6 by 6 grid. Two players take turns covering two adjacent squares by drawing a line. The line can be placed either way: horizontally or vertically. The lines cannot overlap. The game goes on till a player is not able to place any more lines. The player who is not able to place a line loses. With what strategy can one play to win this game?
steps: The centre of the 6 by 6 grid is a corner point where 4 squares meet, so no line can cover it.
Every first-player move has a rotated copy that is free and does not overlap it.
So the second player always has a reply and the first player runs out of moves first.
items.answer: The second player wins: after each move of the first player, place a line that is the 180° rotation about the centre of the grid of that move.
